title: Trump: Most say Trump admin. still hasn't explained Iran goals, CBS News poll finds
description_short: Trump: Most say Trump admin. still hasn't explained Iran goals, CBS News poll finds
description_medium: A CBS News poll after U.S. airstrikes began found that most Americans thought the Trump administration had not clearly explained its goals in Iran. Half expected the conflict to last months or years, and more respondents said the military action would make the U.S. less safe than safer. Two-thirds wanted Congress to approve further action. CBS recontacted people surveyed before the strikes.
description_long: CBS News recontacted Americans who had taken part in a poll completed before U.S. airstrikes on Iran, then compared their views after the attacks began. Most respondents said the administration had not clearly explained its goals. About half expected the conflict to last months or years, and more thought military action would make the United States less safe than safer. CBS reported that people who saw no clear explanation were more likely to disapprove and to expect a long or uncertain conflict. Respondents who believed the goal was preventing nuclear weapons, stopping terrorism or helping Iranians tended to support the action; some instead saw political advantage as the goal. Republicans, particularly MAGA supporters, remained strongly supportive. The poll also found that roughly two-thirds thought Congress should approve further military action. Before the strikes, somewhat more respondents had supported military action specifically to prevent Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons than supported the action in general afterward. The survey records public views and their association with support; it does not establish the administration’s motive or the conflict’s eventual duration.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Most say Trump admin. still hasn't explained Iran goals, CBS News poll finds
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Most say Trump admin. still hasn't explained Iran goals, CBS News poll finds

notes: Read the linked CBS News poll report. The supplied source identifies the recontacted sample, public assessments of goal clarity, expected duration, safety and congressional approval; no exact percentages beyond those included in the report excerpt are added.

title: Protest Masking Criminalization - Facial Recognition Enforcement and Identity Exposure
description_short: Protest Masking Criminalization - Facial Recognition Enforcement and Identity Exposure
description_long: Donald Trump's administration implemented systematic criminalization of face coverings at protests by expanding police powers to ban masks and require identity exposure, using facial recognition technology to identify and prosecute demonstrators while creating 'chilling effects' that deterred disabled activists, religious minorities, and political dissidents from exercising constitutional assembly rights. The masking ban represented weaponization of identification technology against vulnerable protest participants, including disabled activists who relied on face coverings to avoid infection, Muslim women wearing niqabs, and dissidents protesting outside foreign embassies who faced retaliation from authoritarian regimes if identified by surveillance systems. The systematic exposure requirements violated privacy rights and religious freedom by forcing removal of face coverings during protests, with police empowered to arrest anyone refusing to comply while legal exemptions for religious or health reasons were only available after arrest, ensuring widespread detention of innocent individuals. The protest masking criminalization aligned with global authoritarian tactics, with countries like Hungary using facial recognition to enforce bans on LGBTQ+ Pride events by identifying participants for fines and imprisonment, demonstrating how identification requirements served to restrict civic freedoms and intensify exclusion of marginalized communities. Trump's masking ban represented what civil liberties organizations called continuation of 'wave of anti-protest laws that are shutting down ways we can speak up,' following previous restrictions on 'noisy' protests and vague locking-on laws that gave police 'almost-unlimited powers to crack down on protests and arrest demonstrators.' The facial recognition enforcement violated Fourth Amendment protections against unreasonable surveillance while creating systematic intimidation designed to prevent political participation by vulnerable communities who required anonymity protection to safely exercise constitutional rights without facing retaliation, persecution, or violence.

title: Trump defends immigration crackdown at State of Union as approval ratings plummet
description_short: Trump defends immigration crackdown at State of Union as approval ratings plummet
description_medium: At the Feb. 24, 2026, State of the Union, Trump defended his immigration crackdown by citing crimes committed by undocumented immigrants and praising border security. The Los Angeles Times noted that he did not mention Renee Good or Alex Pretti, U.S. citizens killed by immigration agents. Recent polls cited in the report showed low approval of his immigration policy and concern about ICE’s aggressiveness.
description_long: During his Feb. 24, 2026, State of the Union address, Trump defended immigration enforcement by calling the border the strongest and most secure in U.S. history and highlighting people killed by undocumented immigrants. The Los Angeles Times reported that he did not mention Renee Good or Alex Pretti, two U.S. citizens shot and killed by immigration agents in Minneapolis. Rep. Mark DeSaulnier said he was thinking of them and people who had died in ICE custody. The article cited a Feb. 17 Reuters/Ipsos poll in which 38% said Trump was doing a good job on immigration and a Fox News poll in which 59% said ICE was too aggressive. Trump also said the country would continue to admit people legally, while the report noted that his administration had revoked humanitarian protections for hundreds of thousands and indefinitely paused asylum applications filed with USCIS. The speech included guests with sharply different views of deportation policy, and more than 30 congressional Democrats boycotted it. These details show how Trump presented the crackdown amid declining approval and criticism of its human consequences; the cited polls measure public opinion, not the legality of specific enforcement actions.

title: Trump defends tariffs in pre-midterms appearance in battleground Georgia
description_short: Trump defends tariffs in pre-midterms appearance in battleground Georgia
description_medium: At a Feb. 19 event at Coosa Steel in Rome, Georgia, Trump defended his tariffs while a Supreme Court case over the policy was pending. The Guardian said the trip was billed around the economy, but he spent much of his remarks repeating unsubstantiated claims that Democrats use mail ballots to cheat and oppose voter ID. The article noted that mail-voting fraud is exceptionally rare.
description_long: Trump spoke at Coosa Steel Corporation in Rome, Georgia, on Feb. 19, 2026, defending tariffs as a way to strengthen U.S. manufacturing while waiting for the Supreme Court to decide a challenge to his trade policy. The Guardian reported that he called tariffs his favorite word and blamed people he described as aligned with China and Canada for the lawsuit. Although the appearance was intended to promote the economy, much of his speech turned to voting. Trump said Democrats opposed voter ID because they wanted to cheat, asserted that mail ballots enabled fraud, and demanded photo identification and proof of citizenship. The Guardian noted that mail-voting fraud is exceptionally rare and that Trump offered no evidence for his claims. He also discussed the Save America Act, which had passed the House but was unlikely to advance in the Senate without ending the filibuster; the bill would restrict mail voting and impose identification and registration requirements. Trump further attacked an FBI investigation involving 2020 election materials in Fulton County, relying on claims that the Guardian said were debunked. The article documents the remarks and pending policy disputes, not proof of election fraud or a Supreme Court ruling on tariffs.

preserved_fields.title: Trump defends tariffs in pre-midterms appearance in battleground Georgia
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump defends tariffs in pre-midterms appearance in battleground Georgia

title: Trump: Climate leaders condemn Trump EPA’s biggest rollback yet: ‘This is corruption’
description_short: Trump: Climate leaders condemn Trump EPA’s biggest rollback yet: ‘This is corruption’
description_medium: Climate advocates gathered outside the EPA as the Trump administration prepared to repeal the 2009 endangerment finding, which underpins federal climate rules. Senator Sheldon Whitehouse called the move “corruption,” and environmental groups promised court challenges. The EPA said the rollback would save $1.3 trillion but did not explain its calculation; the finding had not yet been rescinded when the Guardian reported.
description_long: The Guardian reported on Feb. 12, 2026, that the Trump administration planned to repeal the Environmental Protection Agency’s 2009 endangerment finding, the legal basis for federal greenhouse-gas regulation under the Clean Air Act. At a rally outside EPA headquarters, Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse called the rollback “corruption” and accused the agency of serving fossil-fuel interests. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin and Trump were expected to finalize the rescission the following day, according to White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt. The administration called it the largest deregulatory action in U.S. history and projected $1.3 trillion in savings, but the report said officials had not explained how they calculated that figure. Environmental organizations including the Natural Resources Defense Council, Earthjustice and the Sierra Club promised litigation. The finding rested on scientific research about greenhouse-gas pollution and had been upheld in federal courts, the article reported. Former EPA officials said the scientific evidence had grown stronger rather than changed. At publication, the repeal was a planned action and legal challenges were prospective; the report did not describe a final court ruling on the proposed rollback.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Climate leaders condemn Trump EPA’s biggest rollback yet: ‘This is corruption’
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Climate leaders condemn Trump EPA’s biggest rollback yet: ‘This is corruption’
